evidence.snippet: Offline pull request export uses core `PullRequestMembership.storedOwnership` alongside its last membership snapshot. It includes saved members and later conclusively owned rounds from all stores; new unknown candidates stay excluded. Eligible raw stores include the own pull store and stores holding saved or newly owned members. A saved member with explicit foreign ownership causes typed refusal before rendering or writing; refresh and `--accept` retain the audit authority. Before the first snapshot, compatibility export reads only the own pull store and excludes explicitly foreign attributed records. An absent own store reports no snapshot without opening another store or creating its own SQLite file. Added records follow saved members in round-ID order without snapshot numbers. Only actual additions cause an escaped stderr notice and Markdown as-of note. JSON membership and history stay exactly as saved, with no new fields or writes. [The offline ownership amendment](../decisions/2026-10-27-offline-export-stored-ownership.md) records the scope.

Export never changes the saved snapshot or history, assigns new membership numbers, or creates a snapshot version. Saved attributed members retain their order; new owned attributed records follow in round-ID order. Raw records keep their existing order. When the selected entries actually add records beyond the snapshot-only selection, stderr names the saved version and the refresh command. Markdown also labels the snapshot's stored time and says the additional records have no snapshot numbers. A candidate without an added export record causes no warning. The notice also covers raw-only additions and makes no claim about their timestamps.

verification.reason: At base, export ordered added rounds by plain ID sort (`.sort()`). Head sorts them with `byMinting`: legacy rounds first by date, then minted rounds by mint time, then ID. Both `docs/guidelines/cli.md` line 42 and the decision doc still say added records follow "in round-ID order". Neither mentions minting order. The doc is stale for the new ordering. In the claim's example, r9 (09:00) then r10 (10:00) is also numeric ID order, so only the "expects r10 then r9" part is a stretch. The doc and the code still disagree for any rounds whose mint order differs from ID order.

The boundary check at compare.ts:363 (`last <= lines.length`) is only tested with line 2 (accepted) and line 400 (rejected) in a nine-line file. Changing it to `<` would reject a miss on the final line, and no test would fail. The truncated branch ("a lens reads only the first") has no test at all.

evidence.snippet: Measuring which routes to commit, the goldens from this week's probes and the `needs-execution` misses, is the issue's second part.

**Misses to replay.** `melian compare misses` writes each valid miss as a case the measurement tool reviews again, in the shape `MELIAN_EVAL_MISSES` reads: the clone, the round's base and head, the file and the external finding's lines. A change to a lens's wording or the harness can then be tried against every real miss so far. A miss with no lines at the compared head cannot be a case, and the command says which and why. [Issue #559](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/559) adds the cause of each miss and the evidence behind it.

verification.reason: The active decision (2026-10-27-offline-export-stored-ownership.md:15) says saved members keep their order and "new owned attributed records follow in round-ID order". The base code did this: `[...owned].filter(...).sort()` orders by ID string. The head replaces it with `.sort(byMinting)` (pull-request-comparison.ts:200-203). `byMinting` (pipeline/src/pull-request-rounds.ts:227-236) orders by `mintedAt`, then by ID only as a tiebreak. So added rounds with different mint times are no longer in ID order. I found no head decision or doc that amends the clause; searching docs for "minted" and "minting" returned nothing. The head's own test, `orders added owned rounds by when they were minted`, asserts the new order and so encodes the departure. The scenario is real: with `r9` minted at 09:00 and `r10` at 10:00, the head emits `r9, r10`, while ID order puts `r10` first. The effect is limited to the order of added records in the export. Only a repeated external ID that matches in one round and misses in another would show a different result.

evidence.snippet:
- Recall counts distinct valid groups. A reviewer gets credit only for its own report judged valid. Precision counts valid reports over valid, noise, and duplicate reports.
- An unadjudicated report is pending and enters neither metric.
- An external-only group whose valid reports all say `out-of-scope` stays outside Melian's recall denominator.
- An empty denominator gives 1, with the raw counts beside it. Reviewers aggregate by name and case-folded login, ignoring version.
- Earlier rounds stay in their statistics. A repeat on a second pull request is a candidate check. `melian compare stats` counts changesets as a stand-in, so two detached rounds of one pull request can still show as a candidate: a known gap, not policy.
- Withdrawing a finding leaves its history stored but removes it from that round's summaries.
- A group with conflicting miss reasons uses the first in-scope reason in site order, falling back to `out-of-scope`. Each defect contributes one miss. Titles that normalise to no letters or digits do not form repeat clusters.
- The drain counts each changeset once. At three or more comparisons, remaining debt keeps the drain due, including after a missed threshold. Local state cannot prove which backlog pull requests shipped or which live runs passed.

verification.reason: The code does what the claim says. `misses()` flat-maps `group.external` and keeps each valid finding, so two reviewers' valid reports at one site give two cases. The cited baseline doesn't forbid that. "Each defect contributes one miss" sits in a bullet about `melian compare stats`, where a group with conflicting miss reasons resolves to one reason. It governs recall counting and the reason tally. It doesn't govern the new replay export, which `misses()` backs through `ComparisonExport.misses`. Nothing at base mentions `compare misses` or `misses()`; both are new at head. The base text the claim relies on therefore never required one replay case per defect. The head's own docs describe the export as one case per valid external finding. That is head text under review, so I rely on it only as a pointer. Whether two cases for one defect is good measurement design is a fair question. It isn't a contradiction of a documented decision.
